lesson.title: Spotting the Outside Function and the Inside Function
lesson.summary: Before applying any chain rule, you need to identify which operation happens last, the outside function, and which happens first, the inside function, since the chain rule always differentiates outside-at-inside times inside-derivative.
lesson.body:
The hardest part of the chain rule is rarely the multiplication step, it is deciding what to call f and what to call g in the first place. Every composite function can be described by asking: if I were plugging a specific number into this expression, what is the very last operation I would perform. That last operation is the outside function; everything computed before that point, to produce the input to that last operation, is the inside function. This order of operations test works for any expression, no matter how it is typeset, because a calculator has to perform the operations in some definite sequence regardless of notation.

Take (x^2 + 1)^7. If x = 2, you would first compute x^2 + 1 = 5, then raise that result to the 7th power. Raising to the 7th power is the last operation, so the outside function is f(t) = t^7, and the inside function, the thing that got raised to the 7th power, is g(x) = x^2 + 1. The same logic applies to sqrt(4x - 1): the last operation is taking a square root, so f(t) = sqrt(t) is outside and g(x) = 4x - 1 is inside. Contrast this with 4x^2 - 1, which has no composition at all in the relevant sense, since it is simply a difference of two terms and each piece differentiates on its own with the sum and power rules.

Consider y = e^(sin(x)). Plugging in a number, you would first compute sin(x), then raise e to that result. So the outside function is f(t) = e^t and the inside function is g(x) = sin(x). Using the composition derivative rule, f'(t) = e^t so f'(g(x)) = e^(sin(x)), and g'(x) = cos(x), giving dy/dx = e^(sin(x)) cos(x). Check with Leibniz notation: let u = sin(x), so y = e^u. Then dy/du = e^u and du/dx = cos(x), so dy/dx = e^u cos(x) = e^(sin(x)) cos(x), the identical result reached a second way. Notice that sin(e^x) is a different composition entirely, with the roles of inside and outside reversed, and it differentiates to cos(e^x) times e^x, a reminder that order matters when naming f and g.

Some expressions have more than two layers, which is where recognizing composition becomes essential before ever reaching for the multiple chain rule; you have to peel back one operation at a time, always asking what happens last. A useful habit: rewrite radicals as fractional exponents and rewrite 1 over an expression as a negative exponent before identifying the outside function, since t^(1/2) and t^(-1) are easier to differentiate than a radical sign or a fraction bar once you reach the power chain rule. It also helps to read an expression out loud the way you would describe it to someone over the phone, since the last word you say usually names the outside operation.

Misidentifying inside and outside functions is the single most common source of chain rule errors, more than arithmetic mistakes made in the multiplication step. Practicing this identification step alone, without even computing derivatives, builds the pattern recognition that every remaining topic in this chapter depends on, from the power, trig, exponential, and log chain rules through the more elaborate multiple chain rule and combining chain rule problems still to come.
